result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.preferential_attachment()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Compute preferential attachment score for node pairs. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L11013-L11091){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.preferential_attachment(ebunch=None) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Preferential attachment](/assets/graphs/preferential-attachment.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Nodes B and E are outlined in the accent color and every edge touching them is in accent; badges give B degree 3 and E degree 4. Shared neighbors play no role: the card multiplies the two degrees, 3 times 4, for a score of 12." width="100%"} For each pair of nodes `(u, v)`, computes `|N(u)| × |N(v)|`, the product of their degrees. Based on the "rich get richer" principle where high-degree nodes are more likely to acquire new connections. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ebunch]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[tuple[Union[int, str], Union[int, str]]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : List of node pairs to compute predictions for. Each pair can use node IDs (integers) or labels (strings). If `None`, computes for all pairs of nodes that are not already connected. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[tuple[int, int, int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of `(u, v, score)` tuples where `score` is `degree(u) × degree(v)`. Results are returned with node IDs. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Preferential attachment scores a pair by the product of their degrees: $\mathrm{PA}(u, v) = |N(u)| \cdot |N(v)|$. It uses no local structure at all, just two degree lookups, which makes it $O(1)$ per pair, and it embodies the Barabási-Albert "rich get richer" dynamic that produces scale-free networks. As a link predictor it works well where degree distributions are heavy-tailed but tends to overrank hub-hub pairs that share nothing else in common. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Since this metric only multiplies degrees, it favors well-connected node pairs regardless of whether they share any actual neighbors -- both nodes here connect to the hub, but node `6` is isolated, so pairing with it always scores `0`: ::: {#97ae94d2 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph(directed=False) # Create network with varying degrees graph.add_star_graph(5) # Hub node 1 with degree 4 graph.add_node() # Node 6, isolated graph.preferential_attachment([(2, 3), (2, 6)]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [(2, 3, 1), (2, 6, 0)] ``` ::: ::: Because it ignores neighborhood overlap entirely, preferential attachment can rank a pair highly even when they share zero common neighbors -- removing one edge from a complete graph still leaves both endpoints with plenty of neighbors in common, so the two metrics tell different stories: ::: {#8bc65b5b .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph(directed=False) graph.add_full_graph(5) # Complete graph K5 graph.delete_edge(source=1, target=2) # Remove one edge pairs = [(1, 2)] graph.common_neighbors(pairs)[0][2] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 3 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#c35701c9 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.preferential_attachment(pairs)[0][2] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 9 ``` ::: :::
